title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: The ability of the eye's lens to change its focal length is called:
questions.solution:
**Accommodation.** The ciliary muscles change the curvature of the lens, so near and distant objects both come into focus on the retina.

A camera does the same job by moving the lens; the eye instead changes its shape.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: Myopia (short sight) is corrected by using:
questions.solution:
In myopia the image forms **in front of** the retina, because the eyeball is too long or the lens too powerful.

A **concave (diverging) lens** spreads the light a little before it enters the eye, pushing the image back onto the retina.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: The splitting of white light into its component colours is called:
questions.solution:
**Dispersion**, and it happens because different colours travel at **different speeds** in glass, so each is bent by a different amount.

**Violet bends most, red least** — the order that produces VIBGYOR.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: The sky appears blue because of:
questions.solution:
Air molecules are very small, and small particles scatter **short** wavelengths far more strongly.

Blue light is scattered all over the sky and reaches your eye from every direction; red passes straight through.

The same effect, with the light travelling a much longer path through the atmosphere, makes the sun red at sunrise and sunset — all the blue has been scattered away before it reaches you.
options: scattering of shorter wavelengths by air molecules

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: The least distance of distinct vision for a normal human eye is about:
questions.solution:
About **$25$ cm** for a normal adult eye, and it is the closest distance at which the eye can focus comfortably.

For a young child it is nearer $7$–$8$ cm, and it moves further out with age as the lens stiffens — which is why older people hold a newspaper at arm's length.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: A myopic person cannot see beyond $50$ cm. Find the power (in dioptres) of the correcting lens.
questions.solution:
The lens must bring an object at infinity to an image at the far point, $50$ cm away, on the same side.

$f = -50$ cm $= -0.5$ m.

$P = \dfrac{1}{-0.5} = \mathbf{-2}$ D — a concave lens, as the sign says.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: How many colours are there in the visible spectrum of white light (VIBGYOR)?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{7}$ — violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red.

In truth the spectrum is continuous; Newton chose seven names, apparently to match the notes of a musical scale.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: A hypermetropic person has a near point of $50$ cm. What power (in dioptres) of lens is needed to read at the normal $25$ cm?
questions.solution:
The lens must make an object at $25$ cm appear to be at $50$ cm.

$u = -25$ cm, $v = -50$ cm.

$\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{-50} - \dfrac{1}{-25} = \dfrac{-1 + 2}{50} = \dfrac{1}{50}$ cm$^{-1}$.

$f = +50$ cm $= +0.5$ m, so $P = \mathbf{+2}$ D — a convex lens.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: What is the angle of a typical equilateral glass prism, in degrees?
questions.solution: $\mathbf{60°}$ — all three angles of an equilateral triangle.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: For about how many seconds does an image persist on the retina (give the answer as a fraction of a second, i.e. $1/x$: find $x$)?
questions.solution:
About $\tfrac{1}{16}$ of a second, so $x = \mathbf{16}$.

This is **persistence of vision**, and it is why a rapid series of still pictures looks like continuous motion — the whole basis of cinema.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: Describe the three common defects of vision, their causes and their correction.
questions.solution:
**1. Myopia (short sight).** Distant objects look blurred; the far point has moved in from infinity.

*Cause:* the eyeball is too long, or the lens too curved, so the image forms **in front of** the retina.

*Correction:* a **concave (diverging)** lens of the right negative power.

**2. Hypermetropia (long sight).** Near objects look blurred; the near point has moved out beyond $25$ cm.

*Cause:* the eyeball is too short, or the lens too flat, so the image would form **behind** the retina.

*Correction:* a **convex (converging)** lens of positive power.

**3. Presbyopia.** Both near and distant vision are affected, and it comes with age.

*Cause:* the ciliary muscles weaken and the lens stiffens, so the eye loses its power of **accommodation**.

*Correction:* **bifocal** lenses — concave in the upper half for distance, convex in the lower half for reading.

**Also: astigmatism**, where the cornea is not perfectly spherical, so vertical and horizontal lines cannot both be in focus at once. Corrected with a **cylindrical** lens.

A cataract — the lens going cloudy — is not a refractive defect and cannot be fixed with spectacles; it needs surgery.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: Explain dispersion of light through a prism and how a rainbow is formed.
questions.solution:
**Dispersion through a prism.** White light entering a glass prism is split into a band of seven colours, a **spectrum**.

*Why:* each colour travels at a slightly different speed in glass, so each has a slightly different refractive index and is bent by a different amount. **Violet is slowed most and bends most; red least.**

A second, inverted prism recombines the colours into white light — Newton's experiment, which proved the colours were in the light all along and not created by the glass.

**A rainbow.** Every raindrop acts as a tiny prism, in three steps:

1. **Refraction and dispersion** as light enters the drop.

2. **Total internal reflection** off the back of the drop.

3. **Refraction again** as the light leaves, spreading the colours further.

The light emerges at about $42°$ to the direction it came from, which is why a rainbow is always an arc of fixed radius.

**Always with your back to the sun** — that is the geometry, not a coincidence. And because each observer sees the light from a different set of drops, no two people ever see quite the same rainbow.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: Explain the scattering of light and use it to account for the blue sky, the red sun at sunrise and sunset, and the choice of red for danger signals.
questions.solution:
**Scattering.** Light falling on very small particles is sent off in all directions. How strongly depends sharply on wavelength: **shorter wavelengths scatter far more** (Rayleigh's law, with scattering proportional to $1/\lambda^{4}$).

**Why the sky is blue.** Air molecules are far smaller than the wavelength of light, so they scatter blue strongly and red hardly at all.

The scattered blue reaches your eye from every part of the sky, so the whole sky glows blue. On the Moon, with no atmosphere, the sky is black even in daylight.

**Why the sun is red at sunrise and sunset.** Near the horizon, sunlight travels through a much greater thickness of atmosphere. Almost all the blue is scattered out along the way, and what survives the journey is red and orange.

At noon the path is shortest and the sun looks white.

**Why danger signals are red.** Red is scattered **least**, so it travels furthest through fog, mist, rain and dust.

A red light is visible from further away, and in worse weather, than any other colour — which is why stop signals, brake lights and warning lamps are red.

**Tyndall effect.** Scattering also makes a beam of light visible — sunlight through a canopy of trees, or a torch beam in a dusty room.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: Describe the structure of the human eye and the function of each main part.
questions.solution:
**Cornea** — the transparent front window. Most of the eye's bending of light happens here, not at the lens.

**Iris** — the coloured ring, a muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the pupil.

**Pupil** — the opening that lets light in. It narrows in bright light and widens in dim light, which is why a room seems dark for a moment when you come in from the sun.

**Crystalline lens** — provides the fine focusing, by changing shape under the ciliary muscles. This is **accommodation**.

**Ciliary muscles** — contract to make the lens more curved for near objects; relax for distant ones.

**Retina** — the light-sensitive screen at the back, holding **rods** (sensitive in dim light, no colour) and **cones** (colour vision, needing bright light).

**Optic nerve** — carries the signals to the brain.

**Blind spot** — where the optic nerve leaves; there are no receptors there, so nothing is seen at that point. The brain fills in the gap so convincingly that nobody notices.

**The image on the retina is real, inverted and diminished.** The brain turns it the right way up — and it learns to. In experiments with inverting spectacles, the world eventually appears upright again.

questions.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
questions.q: What is atmospheric refraction? Use it to explain twinkling stars, the advanced sunrise and the fact that planets do not twinkle.
questions.solution:
**Atmospheric refraction.** The air is not uniform: its density varies with temperature and height, so light passing through it bends continuously rather than travelling straight.

**Twinkling stars.** A star is so distant that it is effectively a **point** source. As its light passes through constantly shifting layers of air, the path wobbles and the apparent position and brightness fluctuate rapidly.

That flickering is twinkling.

**Why planets do not twinkle.** A planet is much closer and appears as an **extended** object — a collection of many point sources. Their variations are random and average out, so the total light stays steady.

This is a genuinely useful test with the naked eye: a steady 'star' is usually a planet.

**Advanced sunrise and delayed sunset.** Light from the sun below the horizon is bent downwards by the atmosphere, so the sun is **seen** before it has actually risen and for a while after it has set.

The effect is about **2 minutes at each end**, giving roughly 4 extra minutes of daylight every day.

The same refraction flattens the sun's disc near the horizon: light from the lower edge is bent more than from the upper, so the sun looks squashed.
